articles.title: Glow: Better reversible generative models
articles.summary: We introduce Glow, a reversible generative model which uses invertible 1x1 convolutions. It extends previous work on reversible generative models and simplifies the architecture. Our model can generate realistic high resolution images, supports efficient sampling, and discovers features that can be used to manipulate attributes of data. We’re releasing code for the model and an online visualization tool so people can explore and build on these results.

articles.title: Learning Montezuma’s Revenge from a single demonstration
articles.summary: We’ve trained an agent to achieve a high score of 74,500 on Montezuma’s Revenge from a single human demonstration, better than any previously published result. Our algorithm is simple: the agent plays a sequence of games starting from carefully chosen states from the demonstration, and learns from them by optimizing the game score using PPO, the same reinforcement learning algorithm that underpins OpenAI Five.

Improving language understanding with unsupervised learning
articles.summary: We’ve obtained state-of-the-art results on a suite of diverse language tasks with a scalable, task-agnostic system, which we’re also releasing. Our approach is a combination of two existing ideas: transformers and unsupervised pre-training. These results provide a convincing example that pairing supervised learning methods with unsupervised pre-training works very well; this is an idea that many have explored in the past, and we hope our result motivates further research into applying this idea on larger and more diverse datasets.

articles.title: AI and compute
articles.summary: We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

articles.title: AI safety via debate
articles.summary: We’re proposing an AI safety technique which trains agents to debate topics with one another, using a human to judge who wins.

articles.title: Evolved Policy Gradients
articles.summary: We’re releasing an experimental metalearning approach called Evolved Policy Gradients, a method that evolves the loss function of learning agents, which can enable fast training on novel tasks. Agents trained with EPG can succeed at basic tasks at test time that were outside their training regime, like learning to navigate to an object on a different side of the room from where it was placed during training.

articles.title: On first-order meta-learning algorithms
Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm
articles.summary: We’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

articles.summary: We’ve co-authored a paper that forecasts how malicious actors could misuse AI technology, and potential ways we can prevent and mitigate these threats. This paper is the outcome of almost a year of sustained work with our colleagues at the Future of Humanity Institute, the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, the Center for a New American Security, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and others.

articles.title: Interpretable machine learning through teaching
articles.summary: We’ve designed a method that encourages AIs to teach each other with examples that also make sense to humans. Our approach automatically selects the most informative examples to teach a concept—for instance, the best images to describe the concept of dogs—and experimentally we found our approach to be effective at teaching both AIs

articles.title: Discovering types for entity disambiguation
articles.summary: We’ve built a system for automatically figuring out which object is meant by a word by having a neural network decide if the word belongs to each of about 100 automatically-discovered “types” (non-exclusive categories).

articles.title: Scaling Kubernetes to 2,500 nodes
Block-sparse GPU kernels
articles.summary: We’re releasing highly-optimized GPU kernels for an underexplored class of neural network architectures: networks with block-sparse weights. Depending on the chosen sparsity, these kernels can run orders of magnitude faster than cuBLAS or cuSPARSE. We’ve used them to attain state-of-the-art results in text sentiment analysis and generative modeling of text and images.

articles.title: Learning sparse neural networks through L₀ regularization
Interpretable and pedagogical examples
Learning a hierarchy
articles.summary: We’ve developed a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm that learns high-level actions useful for solving a range of tasks, allowing fast solving of tasks requiring thousands of timesteps. Our algorithm, when applied to a set of navigation problems, discovers a set of high-level actions for walking and crawling in different directions, which enables the agent to master new navigation tasks quickly.

articles.title: Generalizing from simulation
articles.summary: Our latest robotics techniques allow robot controllers, trained entirely in simulation and deployed on physical robots, to react to unplanned changes in the environment as they solve simple tasks. That is, we’ve used these techniques to build closed-loop systems rather than open-loop ones as before.

Domain randomization and generative models for robotic grasping
Meta-learning for wrestling
articles.summary: We show that for the task of simulated robot wrestling, a meta-learning agent can learn to quickly defeat a stronger non-meta-learning agent, and also show that the meta-learning agent can adapt to physical malfunction.

articles.title: Competitive self-play
articles.summary: We’ve found that self-play allows simulated AIs to discover physical skills like tackling, ducking, faking, kicking, catching, and diving for the ball, without explicitly designing an environment with these skills in mind. Self-play ensures that the environment is always the right difficulty for an AI to improve. Taken alongside our Dota 2 self-play results, we have increasing confidence that self-play will be a core part of powerful AI systems in the future.

articles.title: Nonlinear computation in deep linear networks
Learning to model other minds
articles.summary: We’re releasing an algorithm which accounts for the fact that other agents are learning too, and discovers self-interested yet collaborative strategies like tit-for-tat in the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. This algorithm, Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), is a small step towards agents that model other minds.

articles.title: Learning with opponent-learning awareness
OpenAI Baselines: ACKTR & A2C
articles.summary: We’re releasing two new OpenAI Baselines implementations: ACKTR and A2C. A2C is a synchronous, deterministic variant of Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic (A3C) which we’ve found gives equal performance. ACKTR is a more sample-efficient reinforcement learning algorithm than TRPO and A2C, and requires only slightly more computation than A2C per update.

articles.title: More on Dota 2
articles.summary: Our Dota 2 result shows that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

articles.title: Dota 2
articles.summary: We’ve created a bot which beats the world’s top professionals at 1v1 matches of Dota 2 under standard tournament rules. The bot learned the game from scratch by self-play, and does not use imitation learning or tree search. This is a step towards building AI systems which accomplish well-defined goals in messy, complicated situations involving real humans.

articles.title: Gathering human feedback
articles.summary: RL-Teacher is an open-source implementation of our interface to train AIs via occasional human feedback rather than hand-crafted reward functions. The underlying technique was developed as a step towards safe AI systems, but also applies to reinforcement learning problems with rewards that are hard to specify.

articles.title: Better exploration with parameter noise
articles.summary: We’ve found that adding adaptive noise to the parameters of reinforcement learning algorithms frequently boosts performance. This exploration method is simple to implement and very rarely decreases performance, so it’s worth trying on any problem.

articles.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
articles.summary: We’re releasing a new class of reinforcement learning algorithms, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which perform comparably or better than state-of-the-art approaches while being much simpler to implement and tune. PPO has become the default reinforcement learning algorithm at OpenAI because of its ease of use and good performance.

articles.title: Robust adversarial inputs
articles.summary: We’ve created images that reliably fool neural network classifiers when viewed from varied scales and perspectives. This challenges a claim from last week that self-driving cars would be hard to trick maliciously since they capture images from multiple scales, angles, perspectives, and the like.

articles.title: Learning from human preferences
articles.summary: One step towards building safe AI systems is to remove the need for humans to write goal functions, since using a simple proxy for a complex goal, or getting the complex goal a bit wrong, can lead to undesirable and even dangerous behavior. In collaboration with DeepMind’s safety team, we’ve developed an algorithm which can infer what humans want by being told which of two proposed behaviors is better.

articles.title: Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate
articles.summary: Multiagent environments where agents compete for resources are stepping stones on the path to AGI. Multiagent environments have two useful properties: first, there is a natural curriculum—the difficulty of the environment is determined by the skill of your competitors (and if you’re competing against clones of yourself, the environment exactly matches your skill level). Second, a multiagent environment has no stable equilibrium: no matter how smart an agent is, there’s always pressure to get smarter. These environments have a very different feel from traditional environments, and it’ll take a lot more research before we become good at them.

articles.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
articles.summary: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source , php , security , ai , ai-security-research

articles.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
articles.summary: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. articles.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
articles.summary: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements ( Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript . I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here - it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers : pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers : Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage : Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel : combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command : battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes : Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression : heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 ( play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 ( play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases. I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this: v10: Goliath, and agent battles I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be. Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it [...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech The end result is really cool . Your browser does not support HTML video. Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map. Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area. Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map! The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built. There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths: Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units. Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one). Agent battles The other v10 feature is agent battles . In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game? Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...] Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna , and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses. The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here . There are a few more replays like this linked in the README . I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future. v11: Random Maps This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target: Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative. Here's the transcript , and an image Claude generated to show me its work: v12: Multiplayer via sound I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other! This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept: Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals Build a version of that for battledrones Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well! Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game. Some thoughts I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results. Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. This morning ( via Hacker News ) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop . I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project. ... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! A few other observations from this project: Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out. This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached. Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts. Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects. For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay. Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition. I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked. Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe , the Model browser , the Agent vs. Agent debug tool , and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself. Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame). Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt. I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from. Update: Online multiplayer support Earlier in this article I said: Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache! That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead: If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance? Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folder Here's the resulting server . Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io shared-cpu-1x instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time. Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code. I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game. I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative. Tags: game-design , projects , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , vibe-coding , coding-agents , claude-code

articles.title: My obituary for programming
articles.summary: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

articles.title: llm-echo 0.5
articles.summary:
Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say.
{
  "prompt": "hi there",
  "system": "",
  "attachments": [],
  "stream": true,
  "previous": []
}
Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

articles.title: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript
articles.summary:
Inline rendering with document​.currentScript Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. You can use that to drop in a tiny inline <script> element that replaces itself when the page loads: The year is <script>
document.currentScript.replaceWith(
  new Date().getFullYear())</script> If you define a shortcut function like this: $=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n) You get a tiny template language: The year is <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script> Tags: javascript

articles.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
articles.summary: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

articles.title: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
articles.summary: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? Tags: rdf , semantic-web , sqlite , ai , rust , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code

articles.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

articles.title: LaTeX renderer
articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

articles.title: Tree Appreciator
articles.summary: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. articles.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
articles.summary: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before.  [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

articles.title: llm-gemini 0.35
articles.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars , here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles . That's a fun new twist! Tags: google , ai , generative-ai , llms , llm , gemini , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release

articles.title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
articles.summary: If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten. — Geoffrey Huntley , nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left. articles.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
articles.summary:
Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]]
[ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }]
{ * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }]
{ ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. Tags: open-source , profiling , python , sqlite , uv
